introduction-kafka-without-the-headache.core: Amazon MSK runs Apache Kafka as a managed service: AWS provisions brokers across AZs, handles patching, replacement and metadata management, and integrates with IAM auth, encryption, CloudWatch and MSK Connect. You keep Kafka's APIs and ecosystem without operating the cluster's infrastructure.

first_principles.problem: Self-managed Kafka needs a dedicated team for broker failures, upgrades and ZooKeeper.
truths: Kafka is powerful but operationally heavy.
The ecosystem (Connect, Streams, clients) is valuable.

analogy.title: Hiring a managed fleet for your own delivery routes
analogy.story: You decide what goes where; someone else maintains the trucks.
analogy.breaks: Fleet managers decide truck counts with you; in provisioned MSK, you still size brokers and partitions.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: Survives a broker or AZ loss without data loss (acks=all).

check.q: What replication settings give durability across AZ failure in MSK?
check.a: Replication factor 3 with min.insync.replicas=2 and producer acks=all.

zookeeperless-mode-kraft.core: KRaft replaces ZooKeeper with a Raft-based quorum of Kafka controllers that store cluster metadata in an internal log. It simplifies architecture (one system instead of two), speeds controller failover and metadata propagation, and supports far more partitions. MSK supports KRaft mode on newer Kafka versions.

first_principles.problem: ZooKeeper is a separate distributed system to secure, scale and debug, and limits partition counts.
truths: Metadata as a log replicates efficiently.

analogy.title: Merging two committees into one
analogy.story: Instead of the operations team asking a separate records committee for every decision, it keeps its own minutes.
analogy.breaks: Committee mergers involve politics; KRaft migration needs careful version planning.

example.title: Controller failover
flow: ZooKeeper mode: controller re-election + metadata reload (seconds to minutes at scale)
KRaft: standby controllers already have the log → near-instant

check.q: What consensus protocol does KRaft use?

tiered-storage-infinite-retention.core: MSK tiered storage keeps recent segments on broker EBS (primary tier) and moves older segments to a low-cost, S3-backed tier transparently. Consumers read old data through normal Kafka APIs. Retention can be months or years without huge broker disks, and broker scaling and recovery are faster because less data lives locally.

first_principles.problem: Keeping 90 days of events for replay requires enormous, expensive broker disks.
truths: Object storage is much cheaper than EBS.

analogy.title: A newsroom archive
analogy.story: This week's papers on the desk, older issues in the basement archive, all retrievable.
analogy.breaks: Basements need a librarian; Kafka fetches old segments automatically.

steps.label: Effect
steps.detail: 1 day local, 90 days total, small broker disks.

check.q: What does local.retention.ms control with tiered storage?
check.a: How long segments stay on broker local storage before only existing in the remote tier.

msk-serverless-zero-capacity-planning.core: MSK Serverless runs Kafka without sizing brokers or storage: it scales throughput automatically, bills per partition-hour and data, and requires IAM authentication. Limits exist (per-cluster throughput, partition counts, retention caps), so it suits variable or moderate workloads and teams that want no capacity planning.

first_principles.problem: A team with spiky, unpredictable Kafka usage over-provisions brokers that sit idle.
derivation: Use **provisioned** for very high or steady loads.

analogy.title: Pay-as-you-go electricity versus building a power station
analogy.story: You just plug in and pay for usage, within your connection's limits.
analogy.breaks: Electricity scales almost without limit; serverless clusters have throughput caps.

example.title: Choosing a mode
flow: Steady 500 MB/s core event bus → Provisioned

steps.label: Lesson
steps.detail: Serverless for convenience, provisioned for scale.

example.outcome: Kafka without capacity planning where it fits.
